<reason>PRO (Side B) built the cleaner path. Its opening framed the externality (seller keeps the money, 26 states carry the risk) and its first rebuttal turned CON's "system correcting itself" examples into evidence that every "reform" was externally forced and amounted to shutting programs down. CON's strongest move—separating citizenship sales from residency visas—was met directly (on-ramp, Schengen permit, housing inflation), and CON then conceded citizenship-by-investment is "already dying," handing PRO half the motion. On the lawful-oligarch question, CON's sanctions-law answer was undercut by the point that a Union citizen cannot be entry-banned from the Union. Decisively, PRO's convergence argument showed that CON's own reformed model deletes the property route, which was the revenue CON's small-state defense depended on; CON's "it's just branding, so nothing to abolish" reply left the pay-to-skip-the-queue transaction undefended. CON was competent and its residency/citizenship distinction was a genuine pressure point, but it ended up defending a shrinking remainder. PRO's slight clipping and CON's misattribution of the "dying" quote in closing are minor costs on each side.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B4.5/B5.4 convergence move: stripping CON's reformed program to its elements shows it is an entrepreneur visa, and the deleted property route was the very revenue CON invoked—leaving only "pay, skip the queue, receive the document" for CON to defend.</best_rebuttal>
